sources.title: Maddalena Barenghi, Historiography and Narratives of the Later Tang and Later Jin (2017)
sources.note: Direct scholarly dissertation PDF. Introduction pp. 1-5 on mixed Shatuo military networks and Tang connection; chapter 3 accession and history-making; chapter 4 pp. 146-169 rebellion, Khitan intervention and dynastic transition. Uses convention 923-936; calendar endpoint is separately checked.

sources.title: Richard L. Davis, From Warhorses to Ploughshares (2014)
sources.note: Direct publisher PDF preview, including preface and chapter 1, not a claim to reading inaccessible later chapters. Preface xi-xii political management; pp. 14-17 imperial women, pp. 21-24 military adoption. Contents gives Tiancheng reign 926-930. All URLs for this work treated as one budget.

sources.title: Richard L. Davis, Fire and Ice: Li Cunxu and the Founding of the Later Tang (2016)
sources.note: Direct publisher PDF preview. Preface and historical introduction for foundation; printed p. 203 for 926 change of ruler and reduction of imperial kitchen personnel to fifty. No private household diet inferred from palace establishment.

sources.title: Archontology, Later Tang emperors, 923-937
sources.note: Direct chronological table: last reign ends 11 January 937. Used for calendar endpoint only alongside scholarly account of 936 rebellion; not a substitute for historical analysis.

sources.title: Angela Schottenhammer, A Buried Past (2009)
sources.note: Direct original scholarly article, JESHO 52:14-56. Printed pp. 15-17, original excavated epitaph and conflicting official accounts of Wang Du’s family relationship; analysis distinguishes later narratives from material witness. Wang Chuzhi career predates Later Tang.

sources.title: Yamadera Mitsutoshi, Relief of Musicians from the Tomb of Wang Chuzhi (ICTM 2004 abstract)
sources.note: Indexed original scholarly conference abstract, printed p. 120. Direct PDF opening failed. Exact query: "Wang Chuzhi" "musicians" museum. Excavation 1995; fifteen figures including instrumentalists, conductor and dancers; interpretation as transition from Tang banquet to later theatrical music. Only descriptive count and roles used.

sources.title: Jonathan Hay, Tenth-Century Painting before Song Taizong’s Reign
sources.note: Direct scholarly PDF hosted by NYU, printed pp. 291-294. Dates Wang Chuzhi tomb 924; distinguishes tall folding, tripartite, almost-square and horizontal screen depictions. Public prose describes representations, not preserved wooden furnishings.

sources.title: Shanghai Museum, Tiancheng yuanbao
sources.note: Direct museum object catalogue: title 天成元宝, Later Tang Mingzong Tiancheng era, copper, cast, regular script, diameter 23.66 mm, Sun Ding donation. No controlled archaeological findspot supplied. Traditional modern typesetting 天成元寶 corresponds to catalogue characters; literal English gloss is editorial, not a museum quotation.

sources.title: Bank of Japan Currency Museum, Five Dynasties coinage
sources.note: Indexed institutional PDF Japanese text: limited minting in northern Five Dynasties, continued use of earlier Tang Kaiyuan tongbao, Later Tang Tiancheng yuanbao. PDF direct extraction empty and screenshot failed; no visual inspection claimed.

sources.title: National Palace Museum, Exegeses on the Book of Mencius
sources.note: Direct museum entry, historical discussion paragraphs 1-3: Feng Dao recommendation, Directorate of Education woodblocks modeled on Tang Kaicheng stone classics, earlier private printing, loss of Five Dynasties editions. Illustrated item is a Southern Song edition, not a Later Tang original. Museum’s inaccurate Feng Dao lifespan is not used.

sources.title: Qinding Xu Tongdian, juan 1, Later Tang land regulations
sources.note: Direct Chinese text of later institutional compilation, paragraph beginning 後唐明宗天成四年. Reports 929 edict: households state planted area, five-household guarantee, no local official field inspection; 931 edict limits military farming recruitment. Ancient text paraphrased directly; site AI punctuation/English translation not relied upon. Same work chapters combined in budget.

sources.title: Jose A. Canton-Alvarez, A Gift from the Buddhist Monastery (2019)
sources.note: Direct Medical History article, printed p. 481 / PDF page 7. Discusses Tao Gu’s early Song Qingyi lu account of Mingzong and poppy-seed beverage during military shortage. No recipe, dosing, clinical efficacy or broader Song medicinal practice attributed to Later Tang.

proposedOverrides.name: Later Tang
proposedOverrides.summary: A separate Shatuo-led northern dynasty claiming Tang legitimacy, with major printing and administrative initiatives.

index.name: Later Tang
index.summary: The second of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo Turk Li Cunxu, who destroyed the Later Liang in 923 and claimed the Tang name; it also took Sichuan for a decade.

fell.text: Shi Jingtang, with Khitan help, took Luoyang at the start of 937 and founded the Later Jin, ceding the Sixteen Prefectures around Beijing to the Liao.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact seams ID, no aliases. Tang (618-907 historically, coarse HB 700-1000) and Later Liang are distinct existing narratives. Later Jin 936 regime also separate. Coarse site-created polygon is not a surveyed border and does not depict every campaign or governorship change.
batchIdentityNotes.geography: China-seams polygon 923-937, bounds 102-122 E / 32-41.5 N. Public outline caution preserved. Site source itself calls geometry coarse after Tan Qixiang; no new geometry or corrected border claimed.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Most scholarship conventionally dates dynasty 923-936; calendar succession table records last emperor until 11 January 937. Preserve exact existing seams range 923-937 and explain transition rather than forcing a contradiction.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Period coin legend from Shanghai Museum catalogue; modern traditional printed Chinese and modern Mandarin romanization, editorial literal gloss. Date scoped to named Tiancheng reign, 926-930 in Davis contents. No visual facsimile verification claimed.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: No independently established Later Tang household toilet design, universal medical regime or school attendance figure found. Court food anecdote is later early Song testimony; no Song medicine transferred backwards. Wang Chuzhi material is a 924 burial of a leader whose career mostly predates this dynasty.
